name: Hidden heel lifts / insoles

lead: Hidden heel lifts and height insoles are removable inserts that raise you roughly one to three centimetres inside normal shoes, so the added height does not show from outside. The gain is immediate and lasts while they are worn.

The insert raises the heel, lifting the whole body by its thickness. Some are full-length insoles and others are heel cups. Heel lifts have clinical trials for conditions such as mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, but cosmetic use for height has not been the subject of published trials.

paras: People slip them into shoes with enough depth, often choosing thinner lifts for dress shoes and sneakers, and use them with outfits where a platform would stand out. Shoe fit is the main practical consideration, along with keeping them from showing at the heel.
Altering foot position changes loading and fit, and shoes may feel less stable or tight at the heel. Detection is a common concern, and long-term cosmetic use has not been studied in trials.

web.title: A very tall tale about the men in the shoe lifts business (MEL Magazine)

angle.text: Hidden heel lifts and height insoles add roughly one to three centimetres of height while worn, inside ordinary shoes and without the look of a platform. The gain is immediate and measurable; trials exist for medical heel lifts, not cosmetic use.

lead: Hidden heel lifts and height insoles are removable inserts placed inside ordinary shoes to raise the wearer by roughly one to three centimetres without the visible platform of high heels. Looksmaxxers use them to look taller at once: the added height sits inside the shoe, so standing height and the proportion of body to leg change the moment the shoes go on. Shoes with thickened insoles or built-up heels made to make the wearer look taller are called elevator shoes.[1]

Products range from small heel cups to full-length insoles with a graded wedge, in plastic, rubber, foam or cork. Adjustable inserts of about two inches, and shoes that already carry an inch of built-in lift, are discussed on looksmax.org as options, with attention to which shoe styles hide the insert.[2] Some users make their own from materials such as a yoga mat.[3] Companies sell removable insoles that add a couple of inches to any shoe, as well as elevator shoes whose built-in heels and insoles add up to about five inches, according to MEL Magazine.[4]

Height-adding footwear has a long history, from raised soles in ancient theatre to the men's platform boom of the early 1970s.[5] Heel lifts are also used medically: a randomised trial compared heel lifts with calf eccentric exercise for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, and clinicians use them to compensate for leg length differences, including after hip replacement.[6][7][8] Their cosmetic use for height is not the subject of published trials.
infobox: About 1-3 cm (per product claims); adjustable models up to about 2 inches in forum posts[2]; built-in elevator shoes up to about 5 inches[4]
Plastic, rubber, foam, cork; elevator-shoe soles may also be wood[1]
Heel lifts for leg-length difference and Achilles problems[8][6]
Lift Kits, Shoelifter, Tallmenshoes.com (founded 1996), Don's, TALLER[4]
Cosmetic footwear accessory; medical heel lifts are used by clinicians

paras: Lifts are made of plastic, rubber or foam and sit under the heel or the full foot, so the height-adding component is hidden inside the shoe.[1] Wikipedia contrasts elevator shoes with high heels on exactly this point: in elevator shoes the height-adding part is internal, hiding it from observers.[1] Some products are full-length insoles with a graded wedge, others are small heel cups, and some are adjustable in thickness, with removable layers or a screw-type mechanism letting the wearer choose the gain.

MEL Magazine describes two main categories: removable insoles that add a couple of inches to any shoe, and purpose-built elevator shoes with fortified heels and augmented insoles that add up to five inches.[4] Wikipedia's article on insoles describes the insole as the interior bottom of a shoe and notes that many shoes have removable, replaceable footbeds, which is what allows an insert to be swapped in.[9]

Wikipedia also notes that shoes with thickened soles are used for orthopaedic problems, although the term elevator shoe is not normally applied to those.[1] Clinical heel lifts are described as firm, non-compressible inserts intended to add a constant height so the heel does not rub up and down in the shoe, which is a different goal from cushioning.[8] Elevator shoes proper build the lift into the shoe, so the wearer does not need to place an insert; posters on looksmax.org mention shoes that already carry an inch of built-in lift, such as certain designer trainers, alongside separate boosters.[2]

A lift raises the foot inside the shoe by its own thickness, so a two-centimetre insert adds roughly two centimetres to standing height for as long as it is worn. The shoe's outsole and upper stay the same, so the main trade-off is that the foot sits higher and further forward in the shoe, which is why fit and shoe depth matter to wearers.[2] Because the gain is applied to the heel, ankle and calf positioning also changes slightly; the visible effect is on overall stature and leg length proportion.

sections.h: How people use them to look taller
paras: People wear inserts for specific occasions or daily. MEL Magazine reports that customers include men who want to fit in, men wearing lifts for wedding photos or at bars, and people wearing them for job interviews, public speaking or television appearances.[4] Forum users describe pairing inserts with boots, which hide thicker lifts, or with chunkier trainers; low-cut fashion sneakers are said to show a large booster as a visible gap at the heel.[2]

Cheaper options exist: some users cut insoles from a yoga mat to add about an inch.[3] Commercial buyers choose between small heel cups for dress shoes and thicker full-length boosters for casual shoes, according to community threads.[2][10]

Heel lifts are used clinically for Achilles tendon problems and to compensate for leg length differences.[6][7][8] A randomised trial of heel lifts versus calf eccentric exercise for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy examined these inserts as treatment, not as a cosmetic aid.[6] Wikipedia describes them as physical-therapy devices to shift balance and gait for leg-length differences that contribute to knee, hip and back pain, and as a way of reducing stress on the Achilles tendon during healing.[8] It states that a clinical in-shoe lift should not exceed about a quarter of an inch, citing a 2003 osteopathic text, a smaller figure than cosmetic inserts.[8]
Older orthopaedic literature discusses limb length discrepancy after total hip joint replacement, a setting where lifts compensate for a difference in leg length.[7]

Podiatry and sports-medicine literature discusses how altering foot position can change muscle activity and loading, as in a study of foot wedging and low back muscle activity during walking.[11] The effects of larger lifts worn long term for cosmetic purposes have not been studied in trials. A looksmax.org thread asks what happens to the body when lifts are worn almost every day for a long period, reflecting the same open question.[12]

Fit and stability are the practical trade-offs people report: one poster describes a two-inch booster making a shoe look obviously stepped out of.[2] Another reports that homemade insoles felt too tight until adjusted.[3] Dating coach and author Jonathan Bennett told MEL Magazine that occasional use is fine but regular use has many downsides, and that people are very attuned to lifts and may read them as deceptive.[4]

Raised footwear for stature predates cosmetic insoles. Platforms raised important characters in Greek theatre, Roman buskins sometimes had very thick soles, and Chinese men wore thick-soled boots that survive onstage in Peking opera, according to Wikipedia's platform shoe article.[5] Men's platform shoes peaked in the early 1970s, when they sometimes made up around a fifth of men's shoes sold, and glam rock performers made platform boots part of their image before the style faded in the late 1970s.[5] MEL Magazine's account traces height-increasing footwear to medieval stage actors, Persian horsemen and Louis XIV.[4]

Modern hidden-lift brands date from recent decades. Tallmenshoes.com, a family business in Southern California offering about 600 styles, was founded in 1996, and Lift Kits' founder Derek White told MEL Magazine the company created height-increasing insoles after he saw a model stuff insoles into his shoes in Miami.[4] The same piece profiles TALLER, started by an Australian violinist with prize savings, and Don's, which makes shoes by hand for mostly North American customers.[4]

Height insoles are a common low-cost tool in height discussion because they raise apparent stature immediately and can be removed. Forum threads cover which shoes pair well with them, with suggestions such as boots with insoles for a gain of three inches or more and white leather trainers for lower-profile use.[2] Users on looksmax.org also discuss being noticed wearing them and ways to avoid it, including a German-language thread asking whether others have been caught with height insoles.[10]

Within the community, insoles sit alongside other height-appearance approaches such as platform and elevator footwear, posture work and haircut choices. Some users make their own inserts, for example from a yoga mat to add about an inch.[3]

Wikipedia's elevator-shoe article cites a 1977 newspaper piece titled Elevator Shoes A Boost and a Smithsonian Magazine piece by Sarah C. Rich dated 23 March 2013 about height, reflecting periodic press interest.[1] MEL Magazine's feature tells of a woman who found her boyfriend was about three inches shorter than she thought and wore shoes with built-in 3.5 inch heels, illustrating the concealment issue the magazine explores, and quotes Derek White saying his company serves much of the shorter side of Hollywood.[4]

No studies found on cosmetic height insoles. Heel lifts have been studied clinically for Achilles tendinopathy, including the HEALTHY randomised trial comparing them with calf muscle eccentric exercise,[6] which is a different use. Foot wedging has been examined for its effect on back muscle activity during walking.[11] A 1978 paper discusses limb length discrepancy after hip replacement.[7]

lore.intro: Hidden lifts are discussed as the quickest and most reversible way to appear taller, with attention to shoe choice and avoiding detection.[2][10]
